name: Dilma Rousseff
role: Brazilian president (2011–2016); New Development Bank president (since 2023)
summary: Rousseff advocates social protection, strategic public investment and private enterprise within a developmental economy. She supports democratic institutions, privacy, multilateral cooperation and a low-carbon transition; her record also includes fiscal retrenchment, disputed development projects and shifting social-policy statements.

universal-healthcare.rationale: She guarantees universal healthcare and makes strengthening the SUS a central priority.

public-ownership.rationale: She defends Petrobras’s strategic public role while also accepting private infrastructure concessions.

surveillance-ok.rationale: She rejects terrorism as justification for illegal interception and calls privacy indispensable to democracy.

legalize-drugs.rationale: She explicitly said Brazil was not ready to decriminalize any drug.

empower-police-military.rationale: Expands state security capacity and training.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: A 2014 report says she supported existing legal same-sex marriage; earlier remarks distinguished civil unions from religious marriage, leaving the terminology contested.

abortion-legal.rationale: She earlier endorsed decriminalization, later backed limited legal exceptions, and in 2016 refused to disclose a broader personal position.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Implements university and public-service racial quotas.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Promotes Brazilian audiovisual and cultural production.

reduce-immigration.rationale: She defends Brazil’s reception of Syrians, Haitians and migrants from around the world.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: She gives the UN a leading role regulating interstate surveillance and seeks a more effective organization.

open-borders.rationale: In 2015 she calls restrictions on free movement of people absurd when goods and capital circulate freely.

limit-growth.rationale: She champions growth alongside environmental preservation rather than limiting development.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: She demands an ambitious legally binding climate agreement, economy-wide emissions cuts and forest restoration.

expand-nuclear.rationale: In 2026 she explicitly supports modular reactors replacing coal and fossil-fuel plants to provide reliable low-carbon energy.

socialized-markets.rationale: Explicitly supports private enterprise and investment.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Directs strategic industrial and infrastructure investment.

democracy-best.rationale: She endorses defending and improving imperfect democracy rather than burying it.

direct-action.rationale: In her 2016 impeachment fight she names debate, explanation and dialogue within democracy as her means of resistance.

positive-liberty.rationale: Links citizenship to material social rights.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: She defended countercyclical measures in 2016, after endorsing drastic fiscal cuts and reduced investment in 2015.

force-without-un.rationale: She expressly rejects unilateral military intervention without Security Council authorization.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: She says no professional or public field should be restricted because someone is a woman.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: She promotes development of pre-salt oil and its associated industrial investment.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: She describes pervasive gender prejudice and stereotypes systematically distorting judgments of women in authority.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: She supported the Truth Commission and described the failed challenge to torturers’ amnesty as a loss, while accepting the court’s ruling.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Rejects racial, religious and sexual discrimination.

separated-powers.rationale: She explicitly respects autonomous legislative and judicial powers and the federal principle.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: She positively describes Brazil as a multiethnic country living with difference.

party-controls-media.rationale: She explicitly prefers a noisy free press to dictatorship’s silence.

death-penalty.rationale: She explicitly opposed capital punishment even when asked about a brutal murder.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: She demands financing and technology transfer for vulnerable developing countries’ climate response.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: She insists that law is the limit on rulers and that authorities must stay within their powers.

non-intervention.rationale: Affirms non-intervention and negotiated dispute settlement.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Defends the Access to Information Law.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: She proposes partnerships with private health providers within the public SUS system.

suppress-opposition.rationale: She offers cooperation to opposition parties and rejects discrimination against them.

social-market-economy.rationale: She combines entrepreneurial investment with a state guaranteeing universal services and welfare.

online-participation.rationale: Uses internet for public policy participation.

open-government-data.rationale: Publishes spending through digital transparency portals.

capital-controls.rationale: She pledges protection against indiscriminate speculative capital inflows.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: She advocates development finance centered on emerging economies and broader Global South access to resources.

women-suffrage.rationale: She wants future women to become president and political doors opened to all Brazilian women.

national-resource-control.rationale: She calls Petrobras the instrument of Brazilian sovereignty over oil production.

notes: Full programme and multiple complete speeches reviewed across all themes. Her own 2016 defense of Belo Monte is retained alongside climate commitments; critics dispute its social and ecological costs. NDB speeches establish her own later statements, not every institutional policy. Fiscal restraint and countercyclical spending both appear. Abortion and marriage evidence is qualified. Anti-terrorism legislation and partial vetoes complicate her liberty record; no general emergency-powers position is inferred. Targeted family transfers are not adult basic income, and paid domestic employment is not payment for all unpaid care. No inferred answers.
